findings.title: Case-sensitive blocked email lookup allows trivial bypass
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` queries with `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is case-sensitive in MySQL/Postgres. Users signing up with any uppercase or mixed-case variation of a blocked address (e.g. `BAD@spamclub.com` when `bad@spamclub.com` is blocked) will not match the row and will be allowed to register. The blocker emails are stored verbatim by the migration/model and never normalized, so this completely defeats the anti-spam purpose of the new feature. Normalize on insert and/or on lookup (e.g. `Email.downcase` to match how `users_controller#change_email` already normalizes), or store a separate `email_lower` column and index it.

findings.title: should_block? has a lost-update race on match_count
findings.body: The method does `record = where(email:).first`, then mutates `record.match_count` in memory and calls `record.save`. Two concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked address will both read the same counter, both increment in memory, and both write the same value, so one increment is silently lost and `last_match_at` may flicker between the two competing times. Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` (and avoid loading the row at all when only counting), or wrap in a transaction with row locking.

findings.title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regex matches as substring
findings.body: `Regexp.new("@(#{setting.gsub('.', '\.')})", true)` builds a pattern with no end anchor, so it matches `@example.com` anywhere in the address. With a whitelist of `foo.com`, the address `evil@evilfoo.com` matches because it contains `@foo.com`; with a blacklist of `mail.ru`, `evilmail.ru` style strings may similarly match. This is a pre-existing bug carried over from the old `User#email_in_restriction_setting?` but it is now used by the new validator that gates signup, so it is worth fixing here: anchor with `\z`/`$`, e.g. `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})\z", true)`, and validate the setting format.

findings.title: No test verifies case-insensitive blocking
findings.body: All examples use the same string literal for the blocked record and the queried email. The bypass described in the `blocked_email.rb` finding (typing `BAD@spamclub.com` against a blocked `bad@spamclub.com`) is the most important scenario the new feature is supposed to prevent and it is not covered. Add a context where the queried email differs in case from the stored `blocked_email.email` and assert `should_block?` still returns true (and updates the counter).

findings.title: Query method silently mutates the database
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` reads as a predicate (`should_block?`) but has the side effect of incrementing `match_count` and updating `last_match_at` on every call. This runs during every `User` validation, including any path that re-validates a record (e.g. multiple saves, factory builds, or future code paths), and is undocumented. It also means the spec's `should_block?` subject call mutates rows as a side effect of the assertion, which makes failure modes confusing. Splitting the check from the stats update, or at minimum documenting the side effect, would make the contract explicit and prevent future callers from being surprised by extra writes (and by the lost-update behavior described in the concurrency finding).
